Some other declarative elements that might be useful include country and language pickers. But I think adding them at this point would be jumping the gun a little. I'd rather we let people experiment a bit first to see if any patterns emerge.

I'm also wondering if something higher level like [Project Fluent's DOM integration](https://github.com/projectfluent/fluent.js/wiki/DOM-Overlays) would be more useful. Cc @zbraniecki @stasm .

Okay, https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/issues/12146 got me searching here, and I have a concrete proposal.

The general idea is to take inspiration from SVG and let (almost) everything be specified in both CSS and markup. CSS can be used for cascading common parameters (and just generally cleaning up the DOM), and markup can be used for bits unique to each instance. It impacts text display, but most Intl options could be seen as just styling the output.

## Common properties

These can be used on all the below elements. CSS properties share the same name as the attribute itself.

- `locale`: either a Unicode locale string or the keyword `default`. Default is `default`.
    - Set the numbering system via the Unicode extension key `nu`.
    - Set the calendar via the Unicode extension key `ca`.
    - Set the hour cycle via the Unicode extension key `hc`.
- `localematcher`: either `lookup`  or `best-fit`. Default is `best-fit`.

The browser stylesheet includes `html, body { locale: attr(lang); }` to simplify integration and follow existing practice.

Some properties may be borrowed from other elements. In those cases, the CSS prefix is also that of the borrowed element. For instance, "uses `minfractionaldigits` from `<number>`" means that the attribute `minfractionaldigits` carries the same semantics as it does in `<number>`, and that `number-minfractionaldigits` is its corresponding CSS property name.

## Number: `<number>`

This is derived from `Intl.NumberFormat`. Children is text containing a number value, with optional whitespace on either side.

CSS properties are specified as `number-NAME` where `NAME` is the name of the matching attribute.

- `type`: the formatting style, either `decimal`, `currency`, `percent`, or `unit`. Default is `decimal`. It cannot be specified in CSS as it's semantically relevant to its interpretation.
- `currency`: the currency denomination to use. Required if `type` is `currency`, but may be specified in CSS since things like storefronts would greatly benefit from being able to swap currencies using a single central CSS property.
- `currencydisplay`: either `code`, `symbol`, `narrow-symbol`, or `name`. Default is `symbol`.
- `unit`: the unit to use. Required if `type` is `unit`, but may be specified in CSS since stuff like imperial vs metric switches would greatly benefit from being able to swap currencies using a single central CSS property.
- `unitdisplay`: either `short`, `narrow`, or `long`. Default is `short`.
- `minintegerdigits`: an integer from 1 to 21 inclusive. Default is `1`.
- `minfractiondigits`: an integer from 0 to 100 inclusive. [Default is a bit involved - I'll defer to MDN for the long-winded explanation.](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Intl/NumberFormat/NumberFormat)
- `maxfractiondigits`: an integer from 0 to 100 inclusive. [Default is a bit involved - I'll defer to MDN for the long-winded explanation.](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Intl/NumberFormat/NumberFormat) Ignored if 
- `minsignificantdigits`: an integer from 0 to 100 inclusive. [Default is a bit involved - I'll defer to MDN for the long-winded explanation.](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Intl/NumberFormat/NumberFormat) Ignored if `roundingincrement` is set.
- `maxsignificantdigits`: an integer from 0 to 100 inclusive. [Default is a bit involved - I'll defer to MDN for the long-winded explanation.](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Intl/NumberFormat/NumberFormat) Ignored if `roundingincrement` is set.
- `roundingpriority`: either `auto`, `moreprecision`, or `lessprecision`. Ignored and acts as if set to `auto` if `roundingincrement` is set.
- `roundingincrement`: either `1`, `2`, `5`, `10`, `20`, `25`, `50`, `100`, `200`, `250`, `500`, `1000`, `2000`, `2500`, and `5000`. Default is `1`.
- `roundingmode`: either `ceil`, `floor`, `expand`, `trunc`, `half-ceil`, `half-floor`, `half-expand`, `half-trunc`, or `half-even`. Default is `half-expand`.
- `trailingzerodisplay`: either `auto` or `strip-if-integer`. Default is `auto`.
- `notation`: either `standard`, `scientific`, `engineering`, or `compact`. Default is `standard`.
- `compactdisplay`: either `short` or `long`. Default is `short`. Ignored unless `notation` is `compact`.
- `grouping`: either `always`, `auto`, `min2`, or `none`. Default is `min2` if `notation` is `compact` and `auto` otherwise.
- `signdisplay`: either `auto`, `always`, `except-zero`, `negative`, or `never`. Default is `auto`.

## Datetimes: `<datetime>`

This is derived from `Intl.DateTimeFormat` and `Intl.RelativeTimeFormat`. Children is text containing either a Unix timestamp or an ISO timestamp, with optional whitespace on either side.

CSS properties are specified as `datetime-NAME` where `NAME` is the name of the matching attribute.

- `display`: either `relative` or `absolute`. Default is `absolute`. 
- `relativeformat`: the relative formatting style, either `short`, `narrow`, or `long`. Default is `long`.
- `relativenumeric`: whether to use numeric values in the output, either `auto` or `always`. Default is `auto`.
- `dateformat`: the date formatting style, either `full`, `long`, `medium`, or `narrow`. Default is unset. Acts as a macro of sorts to set other options based on what's best for the locale, and is what people should normally be using.
- `timeformat`: the time formatting style, either `full`, `long`, `medium`, or `narrow`. Default is unset. Acts as a macro of sorts to set other options based on what's best for the locale, and is what people should normally be using.
- `formatmatcher`: either `lookup`  or `best-fit`. Default is `best-fit`.
- `timezone`: the time zone name to display as. Default is the local time zone.
- `timezonename`: either `long`, `short`, `long-offset`, `short-offset`, `long-generic`, or `short-generic`.
- `weekday`: the weekday representation, either `long`, `short`, or `narrow`. Default is unset.
- `era`: the era (AD/BC/etc.) representation, either `long`, `short`, or `narrow`. Default is unset.
- `year`: either `numeric` or `two-digit`. Default is unset.
- `month`: either `numeric`, `two-digit`, `long`, `short`, or `narrow`. Default is unset.
- `day`: either `numeric` or `two-digit`. Default is unset.
- `dayperiod`: the day period (AM/PM) representation, either `long`, `short`, or `narrow`. Default is unset.
- `hour`: either `numeric` or `two-digit`. Default is unset.
- `hourtype`: either `12` or `24`. Default is locale-dependent.
- `minute`: either `numeric` or `two-digit`. Default is unset.
- `second`: either `numeric` or `two-digit`. Default is unset.
- Uses `minfractionaldigits` and `numberingsystem` from `<number>`.

## Display names: `<displayname>`

This is derived from `Intl.DisplayNames`. Children is text containing the code to display, with optional whitespace on either side.

CSS properties are specified as `displayname-NAME` where `NAME` is the name of the matching attribute.

- `type`: either `language`, `region`, `script`, `currency`, `calendar`, or `date-time-field`. This is required, or it won't display. It cannot be specified in CSS as it's semantically relevant to its interpretation.
- `fallback`: either `code` to fall back to the input if the tag is missing, or `none` to display nothing. Default is `code`.
- `languagedisplay`: either `standard` or `dialect`. Default is `standard`.

## Durations: `<duration>`

This is derived from `Intl.DurationFormat`. Children is text containing either a millisecond duration or an [ISO duration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_8601#Durations), with optional whitespace on either side.

CSS properties are specified as `duration-NAME` where `NAME` is the name of the matching attribute.

- `format`: the formatting style, either `long`, `short`, `narrow`, or `digital`. Default is unset. Acts as a macro of sorts to set other options based on what's best for the locale, and is what people should normally be using.
- `years`, `months`, `days`: either `long`, `short`, or `narrow`. Default for each is `narrow` if `formatstyle` is `digital`, `short` otherwise.
- `hours`, `minutes`, `seconds`, `milliseconds`, `microseconds`, `nanoseconds`: either `long`, `short`, `narrow`, `numeric`, or `two-digit`. Default is `numeric` if `formatstyle` is `digital`, the value of `formatstyle` otherwise. If a higher component (including `hours`) is set to `two-digit`, it's ignored and acts like it's set to `two-digit`.
- `yearsdisplay`, `monthsdisplay`, `daysdisplay`, `hoursdisplay`, `minutesdisplay`, `secondsdisplay`, `millisecondsdisplay`, `microsecondsdisplay`, `nanosecondsdisplay`: either `auto` or `always`. Default is `always` if the corresponding non-`*display` attribute is present, `auto` otherwise.
- Uses `minfractionaldigits` from `<number>`.

## Lists: `<list>`

This is derived from `Intl.ListFormat`. Children contains a sequence of elements to intersperse with conjunctions, commas, and such, making this strictly more powerful than `Intl.ListFormat`.

> For simple text items, `<span>`s are sufficient.

CSS properties are specified as `list-NAME` where `NAME` is the name of the matching attribute.

- `type`: either `conjunction`, `disjunction`, or `unit`. This is required, or it won't display. It cannot be specified in CSS as it's semantically relevant to its interpretation.
- `format`: the formatting style, either `long`, `short`, or `narrow`. Default is `narrow`.
@bkardell That's pretty much just a subset of my `<number>` proposal.

The [proposal](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/4630#issuecomment-2849303093) upthread seems to start from the `Intl` APIs and mapping them to elements one-to-one to new elements without discussion of proposed `datetime` element vs. the existing `time` element.

The two main points I want to make are:

1. Please start by looking at the HTML `time` element and datetime formatting.
2. Please be super-careful about adding more platform dependencies on display names that would make it harder for browsers to reduce display names data.

More detail:

I think given that we have had the `time` element for a long time _without_ this functionality, I think it would be productive to analyze:

1. What factors have resulted in the Web Platform not already having this kind of CSS presentability of the HTML `time` element? What should be done this time round to cause a proposal to be implemented?
2. Does the `time` element need any tweaks for the proposed CSS to work?
3. For what default means, is it desirable to take the `Intl` defaults as they are on the JavaScript side, should default mean use whatever CSS `lang()` would consider the language to be at that point on the page, or something else? Most notably, short dates with the slash as the separator are rather problematic when day is less than 13. While the hyphen has a rather strong association with with big-endian dates and the dot has a rather strong association with little-endian dates, with the slash, big-endian, middle-endian, and little-endian all occur around the world and, worse, two of these can occur under a single language component of BCP47: en-US uses middle-endian `M/d/y` while en-IE uses little-endian `d/M/y`. If a user whose system is configured to `en-IE` reads a U.S.-made Web site and sees 8/7/2025, how is the user supposed to tell whether they should interpret the date as middle-endian on the assumption that it's written as the author of the page would have written it or interpret it as little-endian, since the page may be adapting dates to the user's locale defaults?
4. What about longer dates that show months as words? If a user is reading a page that differs from their browser UI language, should the words be in the language of the page or in the language of the browser UI in the "default" case?
5. Should the answer for what default means be different for hour cycle? Ireland implies `h23` but U.S. implies `h12`. Hour cycle adaptation is perhaps the most central of datetime formatting adaptations: Systems that only have one pref for customizing datetime formatting provide a 24-hour clock toggle. But if the hour cycle adapts automatically, does it suggest to the user that the short date changed from middle-endian to little-endian, too? (The easy way out of course is to just say that all this is too hard and HTML/CSS shouldn't be second-guessing this stuff, just do what `Intl.DateTimeFormat` does if you don't pass a locale, but is taking the easy spec writing route _useful_ for users and authors here in the context of this feature?)
6. There is reluctance to expose customizations from system preferences (e.g. navigator.language="en-US" user having enabled the `h23` hour cycle in system prefs) to JS, because exposing customizations exposes fingerprinting bits. However, with CSS, it's at least imaginable to try to have the cake and eat it too: For example by formatting a time as both `h12` and `h23` taking the max of the resulting metrics, and only showing one of the rendering without letting the page detect which one. Is that kind of thing a goal or a non-goal here?

As for display names:

What's the use case for having a `displayname` HTML element? From the shape of the `Intl.DisplayNames` API, it looks like the original use case for the API is being able to dynamically render a human-readable label for any BCP47 tag, a) that's a rather niche use case in itself and b) it's a use case in a dynamic context, so while it might make sense as an API, does it make sense as an HTML element?

Display names have two big problems:
1. The category that Web devs want the most is arguably the least suited to delegating to the platform.
2. Display names are harmful for having browser engines support locales that don't make it into global top N for some value of N.

According to HTTP Archive, the most popular category of display names is region. It's unclear to what extent Web developers who use `Intl.DisplayNames` to render region pickers have considered the issues around region naming, but it seems to me that the more a developer has considered the issues, the less comfortable we should expect the developer to be with a scheme where the developer can't review ahead of time how particular regions are called on their site.

For datetime fields and languages when language occurs in a site-provided picker for site language where the site has the capacity to provide the site in, relying on platform-provided display names means that the site is expected to rely on a special-purpose mechanism instead of relying on the mechanism that it uses for all other strings. Chances are that relying on a special-purpose mechanism can easily take more effort than handling the relevant strings the way everything else is handled. Moreover, in the case of languages with more complex morphology than English, it's extremely easy to get into contexts where you need something other than the stand-alone form of a word. Consider something that instead of saying the “English” says “In English” and then having the analog thing expressed for other languages in the languages themselves: Consider e.g. “suomi” and “suomeksi” for “Finnish” and “In Finnish” in Finnish. It's extremely easy to fall off the edge of what display names can do. (For datetime fields, I was process-wise too late to [raise](https://github.com/tc39/proposal-intl-displaynames-v2/issues/40) this point.)

I think instead of baking display names into more places in the platform, we should rather work on off-ramps for browsers to ship less `Intl.DisplayNames` data while avoiding breaking the Web as it already exists and uses `Intl.DisplayNames`. Here's why:

When you consider how much data supporting a locale in the `Intl` APIs requires, the display names data is notably large for rather questionable benefit. This means that the more we're doing display names, the fewer locales we can ship data for within a given size budget. I think it is much more important to ship datetime formatting, collation, etc. data for more locales than to ship maximal display names for fewer locales.

By making the size of a locale larger, in a scenario where size budget only allows for top N locales, display names hurt datetime formatting, collation, etc. support for locales that don't make it into top N. Making things work out-of-the-box for a smaller N makes the Web less World-Wide.

For other features:

I think it makes sense to look at number and duration formatting after going through the exercise of what datetime formatting should look like, since the `time` element is already there.

The whole point of list formatting is to be able to adapt user-visible text to dynamic data, so I think exploring whether it makes sense as an HTML element and how exactly should come with more examples than what is given upthread.

@hsivonen I'll respond in multiple sections. It was admittedly a lot to run through.

## Display names

I'm okay with dropping display names if it's a concern. Honestly, when I first found out about the API, it was somewhat confusing, because that stuff is normally in translation files. If the use of `Intl.DisplayNames` is an antipattern (I agree that it mostly is), I agree in that an element shouldn't be added for it.

> By making the size of a locale larger, in a scenario where size budget only allows for top N locales, display names hurt datetime formatting, collation, etc. support for locales that don't make it into top N. Making things work out-of-the-box for a smaller N makes the Web less World-Wide.

I'm guessing you're referring to stuff like low-end smartphones and deeply embedded kiosks that have just enough system resources and network speed to not need something like Opera Mini, but not much else? Kiosks could be addressed through custom builds, but low-end smartphones would be stuck between a rock and a hard place. And I do know KaiOS uses Gecko under the hood, and these phones aren't flush with storage space. 250-300MB for CLDR data isn't much of an issue for desktop, but is most certainly a lot for low-end smartphones running on 3G/4G networks, so I can understand the pressure on size there.

## `<time>` element

I'll start off with this: I didn't realize that `<time>` itself accepted half of my proposal for `<datetime>`. 90% of my HTML knowledge is on the scripting side, as the arcane bits of that are most relevant to my needs as a framework maintainer. (I've been off-and-on the maintainer of Mithril.js for about a decade.) So pardon my ignorance on that. 🙃

To my knowledge, it should be safe to just tack everything I proposed for `<datetime>` and `<duration>` onto the existing `<time>` element, attributes and CSS properties alike. Only exception is that the plural `years`/`months`/etc. for duration periods should probably be made singular, so there's not both `year` and `years` that half-overlap. (There is some precedent of this kind of overloading with `<input>`.)

For the value, you'd just use the `datetime` attribute if it exists and fall back to the element's contents if missing. You'd also have to make one of the attributes required to avoid breaking existing content, and the `display` attribute IMHO is the best candidate to require.

### CSS styling

> 1. What factors have resulted in the Web Platform not already having this kind of CSS presentability of the HTML `time` element? What should be done this time round to cause a proposal to be implemented?

Historically speaking, CSS has been strictly about layout, borders, fonts, and texturing, with list numbering, `quotes`, and `content` sticking out as very unusual exceptions. And even then, `content` only truly worked for `::before` and `::after` at first. Since then, CSS has expanded its content generation facilities considerably:

- List numbering and counters got a major overhaul through the 2010s, adding tons of features.
- `content` gained element replacement ability in the early 2010s.
- `content` gained alt text support for text replacement around 2019-2020 in Chromium and last year in Firefox and Safari.
- `content` gained partial image set support in 2012 in Chromium and Safari, and full support came in 2021 for those two (and 2023 for Firefox).

And more recent evolutions are beginning to seriously make this make a lot more sense than it used to. [The current CSS Generated Content 3 draft](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-content-3/) enriches the capabilities greatly, enough to basically make this polyfillable through mixins.

- There's a new `string-set` property to define named strings, a `content()` function to consume the value accessible via JS `.textContent` or other relevant places to help define that property, and a `string()` function to insert a string by name.
- There's new `target-counter()` and `target-counters()` functions to locate things within the document to then generate based on that. `target-text()` can also select text by arbitrary URL, even by local `#id`. The CSS working group seems to be targeting TOC generation and relative cross referencing with this, but their system does generalize beyond that some. (This part is very underspecified, though, and doesn't seem to have much buy-in.)

> 2. Does the `time` element need any tweaks for the proposed CSS to work?

No. See the note at the start of this `<time>` subsection.

### Defaults

> 3. For what default means, is it desirable to take the `Intl` defaults as they are on the JavaScript side, should default mean use whatever CSS `lang()` would consider the language to be at that point on the page, or something else?

The default should be whatever CSS uses as the default for that particular element. Given this would be through CSS, I feel that'd be the least surprising.

IIRC, `lang` on `<html>` defaults to `en` or `en-US`, and that default should be used.

> Most notably, short dates with the slash as the separator are rather problematic when day is less than 13. While the hyphen has a rather strong association with with big-endian dates and the dot has a rather strong association with little-endian dates, with the slash, big-endian, middle-endian, and little-endian all occur around the world and, worse, two of these can occur under a single language component of BCP47: en-US uses middle-endian `M/d/y` while en-IE uses little-endian `d/M/y`. If a user whose system is configured to `en-IE` reads a U.S.-made Web site and sees 8/7/2025, how is the user supposed to tell whether they should interpret the date as middle-endian on the assumption that it's written as the author of the page would have written it or interpret it as little-endian, since the page may be adapting dates to the user's locale defaults?

That IMHO should be up to the user and the browser vendor to work out. The user already configures their system to display dates in a certain way, and this feels no different. And browsers could expose this as an option in their settings alongside stuff like light mode vs dark mode.

Users are already used to dealing with diverging date component orderings online. Confusion between North Americans and Europeans on dates is already a common issue, and it's been like this for almost as long as the Internet itself. Giving an easy way to just show dates in the user's preferred format, with knobs to tweak as needed, would actually help *reduce* this confusion risk - developers are guided to use a single element that forces them to opt into specific methods of display, and in the worst case, users could use an extension or userscript to forcibly opt out of whatever the developer chose.

> 4. What about longer dates that show months as words? If a user is reading a page that differs from their browser UI language, should the words be in the language of the page or in the language of the browser UI in the "default" case?

See above. Same defaults and inference should apply.

Having developers opt into the presentation should be enough to make them aware of what they're doing. And libraries setting the properties and attributes *will* document the fact long dates and times may be translated to users' languages.

> 5. Should the answer for what default means be different for hour cycle? Ireland implies `h23` but U.S. implies `h12`.

No.

> Hour cycle adaptation is perhaps the most central of datetime formatting adaptations: Systems that only have one pref for customizing datetime formatting provide a 24-hour clock toggle. But if the hour cycle adapts automatically, does it suggest to the user that the short date changed from middle-endian to little-endian, too? (The easy way out of course is to just say that all this is too hard and HTML/CSS shouldn't be second-guessing this stuff, just do what `Intl.DateTimeFormat` does if you don't pass a locale, but is taking the easy spec writing route _useful_ for users and authors here in the context of this feature?)

The easy way out IMHO is reasonable. Users can easily configure it and predict the result, and that's the important part.

Do you have examples of 24-hour system toggles that also toggle day/month/year ordering?

> 6. There is reluctance to expose customizations from system preferences (e.g. navigator.language="en-US" user having enabled the `h23` hour cycle in system prefs) to JS, because exposing customizations exposes fingerprinting bits. However, with CSS, it's at least imaginable to try to have the cake and eat it too: For example by formatting a time as both `h12` and `h23` taking the max of the resulting metrics, and only showing one of the rendering without letting the page detect which one. Is that kind of thing a goal or a non-goal here?

I explicitly am *not* proposing any fingerprinting not already possible through a bunch of `:lang()`s and possible `:not()`s.

## Numbers and durations

> I think it makes sense to look at number and duration formatting after going through the exercise of what datetime formatting should look like, since the `time` element is already there.

That's fine. And concerns are similar between the two.

I do feel this could be a simple thing to resolve, though:

- Like `<datetime>` with `<time>`, it's possible to just add everything from my proposed `<number>` to `<data>`.
- `<time>` also supports durations, so it's easy enough to just mix the `<duration>` proposal in with that as we. I've taken the liberty to do so already in earlier discussion.

## Lists

> The whole point of list formatting is to be able to adapt user-visible text to dynamic data, so I think exploring whether it makes sense as an HTML element and how exactly should come with more examples than what is given upthread.

What kind of examples are you hoping for? I'm envisioning something like this tag list implementation:

```jsx
// I'm using Mithril.js + JSX
const TagList = {
  view: ({attrs: {names}}) => <div class="tag-list">
    {i18n.t("tag-list.label")}
    <list>
      {names.map(name => (
        <m.route.Link href="/tags/:name" params={{name}}>
          {name}
        </m.route.Link>
      ))}
    </list>
  </>,
}
```

By the way, you might think it's possible to just use `Intl.ListFormat.prototype.formatToParts`, but [that stringifies its arguments](https://tc39.es/ecma402/#sec-Intl.ListFormat.prototype.formatToParts). In fact, [its parts generation is sensitive to the text content of its entries](https://tc39.es/ecma402/#sec-createpartsfromlist). You could hack it to work with objects, but it'd be awkward and clumsy.

The idea is to do similar in HTML/CSS, but based on the `.textContent` of each inner child. And this cannot be efficiently polyfilled in HTML without basically just reimplementing `Intl.ListFormat` itself.

There are some examples of declarative custom elements around the Intl API:

From the Shoelace design system:
- https://shoelace.style/components/format-bytes
- https://shoelace.style/components/format-date
- https://shoelace.style/components/format-number
- https://shoelace.style/components/relative-time

I haven't done any research, but i'm sure these are not the only examples.

> > By making the size of a locale larger, in a scenario where size budget only allows for top N locales, display names hurt datetime formatting, collation, etc. support for locales that don't make it into top N. Making things work out-of-the-box for a smaller N makes the Web less World-Wide.
> 
> I'm guessing you're referring to stuff like low-end smartphones and deeply embedded kiosks that have just enough system resources and network speed to not need something like Opera Mini, but not much else?

No, I'm referring to Firefox and Chrome, which unlike Safari, ship their own copies of i18n data and code.

Chrome already has a history of subsetting CLDR data on a "top N" basis. My go-to example is Cherokee collation. Try `console.log(["Ꮑ", "a"].sort(new Intl.Collator("chr").compare));` in Firefox, Safari, and Chrome. Firefox and Safari put Cherokee before Latin. The Cherokee collation data is tiny: It just a script reordering on top of the root collation (like for e.g. for Greek) to decide cross-script comparisons as Cherokee first. If things were considered on a case-by-case basis for size, it wouldn't make sense to make an effort to drop Cherokee collation, since the size saving is so tiny. However, when applying just a "top N locales" cutoff to all i18n data, Cherokee doesn't get included. Making circumstances that guide toward a smaller N would make this pattern even worse.

At one point in the past, Firefox had a long period of shipping the `Intl` API on desktop but not on Android due to size concerns. While Firefox is not right now at an acute risk of reaching a size that would trigger size concerns on Android, if the size of the browser as a whole gets carelessly larger, at some point someone is likely to say that it's not OK.

When functionality isn't reliably available, it becomes less useful even in cases where it is available, since Web developers can't rely on the functionality working.

> That IMHO should be up to the user and the browser vendor to work out.

I think specs should make some realistic assumption of how the specs would be implemented instead of leaving the hard parts to others to figure out.

> The user already configures their system to display dates in a certain way, and this feels no different. 

Web exposure is different in two ways:
1. Fingerprinting
2. The user can be less sure of whether the user setting is taking effect on a given Web site, so ambiguous cases are worse.

> Users are already used to dealing with diverging date component orderings online. Confusion between North Americans and Europeans on dates is already a common issue, and it's been like this for almost as long as the Internet itself. Giving an easy way to just show dates in the user's preferred format, with knobs to tweak as needed, would actually help reduce this confusion risk - developers are guided to use a single element that forces them to opt into specific methods of display, and in the worst case, 

It's an old problem, yes, but does this proposal make the problem worse or better for a user who, by looking at a date with slashes on an apparently U.S.-originating English-language page can't tell if the date component order is hard-coded by the U.S. page author or if the date component order is adapting to the user's Irish locale settings?

> users could use an extension or userscript to forcibly opt out of whatever the developer chose.

> No, I'm referring to Firefox and Chrome, which unlike Safari, ship their own copies of i18n data and code.

We're experiencing the very same business trade-offs when handling i18n support for our OSes. We are currently running dangerously close to data payload becoming a problem and the leadership response is to cut down the number of locales supported by the OS and the web view shipped with it to a very low number (sub 20).
So, even if you tried to say "how about browsers just use OS i18n data" the answer is - the OSes are struggling to ship with that much data and the problem is only going to become more acute as the form factors variety increases over the next years.

The question of slicing features or locales is at the core of architectural choices that every ecosystem, OS and browser vendor is running through.
By inflating the size as we evolve HTML we will force the hand of many such systems in ways that I don't think we will like.
Please, be mindful of that when considering requesting features that require size marginal (per-locale) size inflation.
